title: Depth through atmospheric post-processing: multi‑zone sky/foreground work and haze in Photoshop (PD Spring 2022)

locations.name: Triangle Reef
locations.basis: explicit mention: “triangle reef on the map of locations that i give you”; later reference to Triangle Reef as a nearby comparison/location

summary: The video presents a step‑by‑step Photoshop workflow tailored for drone/landscape imagery, focused on creating depth and atmosphere. Beginning with a darkened exposure that preserves shadow detail, the presenter separates foreground processing from sky work, then iteratively warps and expands sky elements to introduce leading lines. Color grading is applied selectively to foreground and horizon blues, followed by a dedicated blur plus luminosity pass to generate glow and push midtones back. A core portion of the method is a labor‑intensive, multi‑layer haze build using clone painting and selective erasure (history brush) to simulate atmospheric perspective across distant layers. The timeline moves through multi‑zone adjustments in Camera Raw, targeted saturation and hue shifts, and occasional use of tools like sponge, puppet warp, and perspective warp. The approach emphasizes drawing the eye toward light and creating a three‑dimensional feel by layering and shaping light, color, and atmosphere across depth.

sections.title: Initial exposure, shadows, and foreground/sky separation
sections.description: Set a darker overall exposure while preserving shadow detail. Begin foreground processing and gradually choose to leave the sky alone for foreground tweaks, then prepare for sky adjustments later. The speaker emphasizes that shadows should retain detail to allow recovery from RAW data.

sections.title: Sky shaping with perspective tricks and tiny sky tweaks
sections.description: Apply perspective warp to the sky to create more interesting leading lines; experiment with a dramatic, trapezoid‑like warp and a puppet warp to adjust isolated sky areas without disturbing the rest of the frame.

sections.title: Foreground color grading and horizon blues
sections.description: Process foreground details first, then selectively adjust sky later. Alter blue saturation and luminance to avoid aqua/cyan distortions, apply blues in camera calibration, and introduce warmth to the horizon to balance the scene.

sections.title: Blur + luminosity: creating depth and glow
sections.description: Implement the blur plus luminosity technique to the background, enhancing depth and creating a hazy, distant glow. Balance brightness and warmth, push the midtones to simulate atmospheric depth, and gradually refine the effect across the mid to far ground.

sections.title: Atmosphere construction with clone painting; iterative refinements
sections.description: Use the clone stamp to paint brighter/hazier layers behind key structures (e.g., a tower) to simulate atmospheric layers. Erase and refine mistakes with the history brush, progressively building seven or more atmospheric layers and adjusting hues/saturation per layer to preserve depth while avoiding obvious artifacts.

sections.title: Layer-by-layer refinement and depth storytelling
sections.description: Continue multi‑zone refinement, with notes on haze settling in lower areas and the need to maintain separation between foreground/middle ground and backdrop. Use tools like sponge for localized color tweaks and selective masking to keep edges believable while enhancing depth.

sections.title: Two-zone processing in Camera Raw for complex scenes
sections.description: Demonstrate dividing an image into multiple processing zones (bottom/middle/top) to treat each region differently. Apply dehaze and texture selectively, then blend zones to preserve overall cohesion while enhancing three‑dimensional feel.

sections.title: Directional light emphasis with adaptive distortion and warm highlights
sections.description: Experiment with an adaptive wide angle filter to exaggerate light direction and create a stronger directional pull. Increase brightness and warmth in the upper-left region, then balance with the rest of the frame to guide the viewer’s eye along the light path.

sections.title: Closing perspective: the core takeaway
sections.description: Summarizes the overarching idea: depth and movement in landscape imagery come from consistent transitions (big-to-small, dark-to-light, cool-to-warm) that guide the viewer toward the light and create a layered, three‑dimensional feel.
